evidence: image (left col, ~lines 33-35): 'videnđ est ut[rum] disseisit[us] p[re]sens fuit vel absens tempore disseisine & ut[rum] ipse [presens?] eiciat vel eius p[ro]curator vel familia vel dum absens fuit alius ingrediat[ur] in sua[m] vacua[m] possessione[m]'. OCR: 'praesens sit vel absens tempore disseisinae vel ipse sive canes vel eius paratus vel familia'. 'pcurator' (procurator) is read as 'paratus' and the verb as 'canes'; there are no dogs on the leaf. Translation 'or [his] dogs, or his equipment' misleads on who was ejected (self, attorney, household).

image (left col, under the red rubric 'De primo remedio post disseisinam'): 'ille qui iniust[e] ... disseisit[us] e[st] p[er] se si possit vel p[er] ... viribus vel resu[m]ptis dum t[ame]n sine aliquo intervallo flagrante disseis[ina] vel malefic[io] reiciat spoliante[m]. Incontinenti est vi vim repellere...'. OCR: 'ille qui iniuste eicitur disseisitore praesente et si possit statim et sine intervallo dum tamen cuius sit aliquo intervallo flagrante disseisina vel maleficio recenti spoliantem Incontinenti est viribus repellere'. The page is seriously garbled, but OCR tokens are anchored to the leaf throughout (flagrante disseisina, maleficio, spoliantem, Incontinenti, intervallo, superiorem, xv dies). This is pervasive, meaning-changing misreading of an abbreviated textualis, not confabulation of text absent from the leaf (O1 requires few or no anchored tokens). Serious at page level, so not downgraded.

Translation renders the misread 'ipse sive canes vel eius paratus vel familia' as 'or he himself, or [his] dogs, or his equipment, or his household' with no uncertainty marker; the leaf has 'ipse ... vel eius procurator vel familia'. A reader is told dogs and equipment figure in Bracton's rule.

image (left col, ~lines 19-20): 'ille ad que[m] res p[er] intervallu[m] translata fuit tantu[m] ad restitucione[m] secundu[m] virtute[m] assise ut inf[ra] dicet[ur]'. OCR: 'tunc ad quem res spiritualis translata sunt an ad restitutionem'. 'pīntuallū' is read as 'spiritualis'.

image (right col, ~lines 22-23): 'Est aut[em] ista recognicio sive assisa [com]plexa & pena multiplex ut inf[ra] de restitucione dampnor[um]' (the margin note repeats '& pena multiplex ut infra de restitucione dampnorum'). OCR: 'Est autem ista recognitio sive assisa ex pluribus iunctis in lapis ut infra de restitutione dampnorum'. The phrase is on the leaf and badly misread ('cplex & pena multiplex' -> 'ex pluribus iunctis in lapis'), surrounded by correctly read text; this is a misread, not invention. Still serious: the point that the assize carries a multiple penalty is lost.

Translation: 'him to whom the spiritual things were transferred', from the misread. The leaf says the thing was transferred 'per intervallum' (after an interval), which is the hinge of the passage on second-hand holders. Rendered fluently with no flag.

Translation: 'This recognition or assisa is [composed] from several things joined in the stone'. The leaf has 'complexa & pena multiplex' (complex, and the penalty manifold). A meaningless phrase is translated as law with no uncertainty marker.

image (right col, ~lines 15-18): 'It[em] q[ua]n[do]q[ue] competit villano sokemanno in d[omi]nico d[omi]ni reg[is] si manu[m] vocet burgum ... ut de t[er]ra Albis de Badinge x. an[norum] de Patishull in com. Glouc. anno R. H. q[ui]nto. ass. no. dis.' OCR: 'qui competit villano solemniter in dominico domini regis ... de curia albis de vadinge x. annorum de placitis in eorum gloucester. anno. b. h. quarto.' Sokemanno -> solemniter, Patishull -> 'de placitis', quinto -> quarto: the case citation (justice and regnal year) is wrong.

Translation: 'in the year of King Henry the Fourth'. Even the stored OCR 'anno ... h. quarto' means 'in the fourth year of [King] H.'; the leaf has 'quinto' (the fifth year, Henry III era for Bracton). The rendering creates an anachronistic citation to Henry IV (r. 1399-1413) in a 13th-century treatise.

Translation: 'he who belongs to the villain is solemnly in the lord king's demesne if he harms the borough ... by white rents <note>payments in silver</note>'. The leaf says the assize lies for a villein sokeman on the king's demesne, citing a case from Patishull's eyre. The English is nonsense presented as a legal rule, with an invented gloss.

image: 'Inquinat᷑ eni hoc bonū: admixtione maloꝝ. īfectū vero: vlteri⁹ bonū nō ꝑmanet. sin minime ꝑmanet: malū efficit᷑.' (Inquinatur ... efficitur, both with the -ur sign). The OCR drops both: 'Inquinat enim hoc bonum ... malum efficit.' The translation follows the OCR: 'this good pollutes with the admixture of evils; the good, however, does not remain further infected. If it does not remain at all, it makes evil.' The source says this good is polluted by the admixture of evils; once infected it no longer remains good, and if it does not remain good it becomes evil. The agency is inverted and the conclusion garbled. The middle clause is also a translation error (T8); the O6 root is the dropped -ur abbreviations.

The image and OCR agree: 'Aula choris, epulisq; uacat: nec perdita curant: / Dum superest aliquid.' Translation: 'The court is empty of dances and feasts: nor do they care for what is lost'. With 'nec perdita curant dum superest aliquid', the sense is that the court is given over to dances and feasts (vacat + dative, 'has time for'), as in the standard renderings. The translation inverts the satire of a court revelling while the provinces burn.

image (first line under 'DE LAVDIB. STIL.', zoomed): 'M aius erit. ueteres actus, primamq; iuuentam' (spaced initial M + 'aius'). OCR: 'Madius erit'. The translation then rendered this non-word as 'meager', so the misread changes the meaning.

Translation: 'It will be meager.' The source 'Maius erit' (it will be greater) says that whatever the poet leaves out will be greater than what he tells. The English reverses the sense, built on the 'Madius' misread ('quodcunque relinquam' is on the previous page). It could equally be filed as T7 in the translation lane.
